newsitem.title: UK: DHL sees more east Europe/Russia growth.
newsitem.headline: DHL sees more east Europe/Russia growth.

text.p: Confidence is returning to eastern European economies and markets as inflation slows and currencies stabilise, said DHL regional director for eastern and central Europe and Russia, Peter Davies.

Growth might have slowed in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union after the initial euphoria following the collapse of the Iron Curtain, but the long-term trend remained upwards, he told Reuters in an interview.
"It is important to operate domestically and have one's own locally employed staff," said Davies, who is responsible for east Europe and the former Soviet Union.
Davies said he reckoned that on average DHL held some 60 percent of the eastern and central European express freight business.
Amongst individual countries, its market share probably varied between 95 percent in Albania down to 40 percent in the Czech Republic, with Russia in mid-range at 50-55 percent.
Competition was mainly from its traditional western rivals like UPS, TNT and Federal Express.
DHL hoped to achieve 1997 revenue growth in east and central Europe of over 30 percent against 40 percent in 1996 and was projected to maintain this in 1998, Davies said.
Country growth rates varied, with over 50 percent in Poland and 35 percent in Russia.
Across eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, DHL had found bureaucratic customs procedures to be a hindrance and was currently working with customs and government officials to overcome these.
Exporters from eastern and central Europe were also increasingly arguing for faster customs handling, he added.
At its Brussels hub, Davies said DHL handled 700-900 tonnes a night with 30 customs officers in attendance. In eastern Europe there were many more officials and much more paperwork.
DHL was trying to introduce faster handling procedures in eastern Europe and making use of electronic processing.

Some progress had been made and, as an example, Davies said DHL now handled 1,500 packages a night in Prague compared to 100 four years ago and that this could be increased further with extra training and investment.

Lufthansa and Japan Airlines each own 25 percent of DHL with Nisshono Iwai holding 7.5 percent. Davies said no conflicts arose because of competitive services and he expected these shareholdings to stay unchanged.
